📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service.
  • Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service.
  • Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service. They are solely focused on the result and say, “I could do that with AI.” Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility. We are increasingly seeing this in the architectural industry. And it’s more than just a feeling or a hunch. Recently, the U.S. Department of Education moved to alter the definition of professional degrees to exclude architecture. This demonstrates a serious misunderstanding of what architecture entails. The creative professionals delivering complex projects in the built environment are experts: systems thinkers choreographing designs that shape environments, cultures, and communities. DESIGN AND EMOTION Design decisions are interconnected, but that complexity is often underestimated. Changes made after work is underway can require significant rework and additional layers of coordination, impacting budget and schedule. Even seemingly small change requests can ripple through other systems and affect project value. Behind every built environment is a constellation of decisions and balancing acts that are invisible to the end user. A successful design blends noiselessly into daily life. When everything is working, and spaces are intuitive, comfortable, and almost anticipatory in supporting your needs, you rarely think about the creativity, imagination, and coordination behind each design and engineering decision. Architecture’s value is its ability to make us feel something as we enter a space before we even understand why we are experiencing those emotions. The reverence of a cathedral, the excitement of a stadium, the safety and security of a home—those emotional and physical reactions do not happen by chance. Each response is a specific result of a team’s design decisions. IMPACT VERSUS HOURS There’s an idea that generative AI can replace nearly any profession. This is a tough pill to swallow for those who’ve spent years or decades honing their craft. But this way of thinking raises a deeper question: Is worth measured by the visible impact you create or the hours you log? I know architects aren’t the only ones who experience this. Leaders in finance, medicine, tech, and other fields hear from people who see the tip of the iceberg and don’t realize how much is below the surface. When they don’t understand the extent of expertise, they don’t value it. They think it can be done quickly and simply. The final output is neat and clean. But the reality is that the design process is often complex. It involves researching, discussing, debating, ideating, innovating, finding common ground, and making decisions. One skill an architect learns over time is listening beyond the client’s initial brief, identifying added value to the design program. Early in your career, you treat a brief as a rulebook. Over time, you learn how to advocate for a vision often shaped by a process of listening, challenging, and refining. It’s important for us to embrace productive friction, in life and in this discipline. It’s the moments that must be experienced, including moments of friction when we are challenged and must overcome some adversity, that are more formative and leave a lasting impact. 6 DESIGN AREAS REQUIRING HUMAN SKILLS Consider these six challenging parts of any design process that require human expertise: 1. Consensus building: While AI can pull data from multiple sources, it cannot negotiate and compromise with diverse stakeholders. People disagree. An architect is a bridge between clients, project partners, and city officials. Architects have to balance vision with constraints, and to resolve disagreements and conflicts among all parties. 2. Constructability and feasibility: It’s impressive when AI can generate a beautiful rendering in seconds. But what if the rendering isn’t practical or realistic? Architects must make the design come alive in the real world. They need to know, through knowledge and experience, how a design will perform when built, and to exercise judgment based on wisdom. 3. Intelligence beyond pattern recognition: Despite the word “intelligence,” does AI think? Or does it recognize patterns, relying on existing data to predict future outcomes? As today’s problems grow increasingly complex, the synthesis of this complex data to anticipate outcomes is a powerful tool. Where AI recognizes patterns, architects bring discernment, interpreting data through a lens that is contextual and time-sensitive, creating solutions tailored to the histories and needs of specific sites and the communities that use them. 4. Risk management and resilience: Architects are tasked with thinking about future stressors on a building. Based on historic precedent, they consider what long-term resilience is required of buildings they are designing. AI can’t assume that human element of taking responsibility and accountability. IBM’s training manual in 1979 stated, “A computer can never be held accountable; therefore, a computer must never make a management decision.” AI doesn’t understand that lives will be seriously affected if its design isn’t resilient; it’s imperative to leverage the tool responsibly. 5. Challenge assumptions as a trusted advisor: We want to assume the best of those we work with, but trust isn’t easy to build. It’s built through real-world troubleshooting and problem-solving. Sometimes that means saying no. Anyone who ever had a chatbot agree with everything they noted understands that AI often tells you what you want to hear. 6. Center work around human experience and emotion: Joy Evans Therapeutic Recreation Center in Washington, D.C.—the only public recreation center in the region offering therapeutic recreational programming—exemplifies the importance of designing for a range of human experiences. To make the center a welcoming and inclusive place for people of all ages and abilities, our designers needed a thorough human understanding of what made people feel safe, seen, and inspired. AI can grasp key tenets of accessibility and belonging abstractly, but doesn’t understand human vulnerability. When we recognize and respect these messy parts of the process, we understand that human professionals can’t be replaced. It’s important we help our clients and customers understand this too, demonstrating how we can use the best of AI while emphasizing the value of human judgment and perspective. Steven McKay is CEO of DLR Group.

Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service. They are solely focused on the result and say, “I could do that with AI.”.

Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility.

We are increasingly seeing this in the architectural industry. And it’s more than just a feeling or a hunch. Recently, the U.S. Department of Education moved to alter the definition of professional degrees to exclude architecture. This demonstrates a serious misunderstanding of what architecture entails. The creative professionals delivering complex projects in the built environment are experts: systems thinkers choreographing designs that shape environments, cultures, and communities.

Design decisions are interconnected, but that complexity is often underestimated. Changes made after work is underway can require significant rework and additional layers of coordination, impacting budget and schedule. Even seemingly small change requests can ripple through other systems and affect project value.

Behind every built environment is a constellation of decisions and balancing acts that are invisible to the end user.

A successful design blends noiselessly into daily life. When everything is working, and spaces are intuitive, comfortable, and almost anticipatory in supporting your needs, you rarely think about the creativity, imagination, and coordination behind each design and engineering decision.

In a recent development, architecture’s value is its ability to make us feel something as we enter a space before we even understand why we are experiencing those emotions. The reverence of a cathedral, the excitement of a stadium, the safety and security of a home—those emotional and physical reactions do not happen by chance. Each response is a specific result of a team’s design decisions.

According to recent reports, there’s an idea that generative AI can replace nearly any profession. This is a tough pill to swallow for those who’ve spent years or decades honing their craft. But this way of thinking raises a deeper question: Is worth measured by the visible impact you create or the hours you log?

I know architects aren’t the only ones who experience this. Leaders in finance, medicine, tech, and other fields hear from people who see the tip of the iceberg and don’t realize how much is below the surface. When they don’t understand the extent of expertise, they don’t value it. They think it can be done quickly and simply.

The final output is neat and clean. But the reality is that the design process is often complex. It involves researching, discussing, debating, ideating, innovating, finding common ground, and making decisions. One skill an architect learns over time is listening beyond the client’s initial brief, identifying added value to the design program. Early in your career, you treat a brief as a rulebook. Over time, you learn how to advocate for a vision often shaped by a process of listening, challenging, and refining.

It’s important for us to embrace productive friction, in life and in this discipline. It’s the moments that must be experienced, including moments of friction when we are challenged and must overcome some adversity, that are more formative and leave a lasting impact.

Consider these six challenging parts of any design process that require human expertise:.

Sources indicate that 1. Consensus building: While AI can pull data from multiple sources, it cannot negotiate and compromise with diverse stakeholders. People disagree. An architect is a bridge between clients, project partners, and city officials. Architects have to balance vision with constraints, and to resolve disagreements and conflicts among all parties.

2. Constructability and feasibility: It’s impressive when AI can generate a beautiful rendering in seconds. But what if the rendering isn’t practical or realistic? Architects must make the design come alive in the real world. They need to know, through knowledge and experience, how a design will perform when built, and to exercise judgment based on wisdom.

3. Intelligence beyond pattern recognition: Despite the word “intelligence,” does AI think? Or does it recognize patterns, relying on existing data to predict future outcomes? As today’s problems grow increasingly complex, the synthesis of this complex data to anticipate outcomes is a powerful tool. Where AI recognizes patterns, architects bring discernment, interpreting data through a lens that is contextual and time-sensitive, creating solutions tailored to the histories and needs of specific sites and the communities that use them.

According to recent reports, 4. Risk management and resilience: Architects are tasked with thinking about future stressors on a building. Based on historic precedent, they consider what long-term resilience is required of buildings they are designing. AI can’t assume that human element of taking responsibility and accountability. IBM’s training manual in 1979 stated, “A computer can never be held accountable; therefore, a computer must never make a management decision.” AI doesn’t understand that lives will be seriously affected if its design isn’t resilient; it’s imperative to leverage the tool responsibly.

In a recent development, 5. Challenge assumptions as a trusted advisor: We want to assume the best of those we work with, but trust isn’t easy to build. It’s built through real-world troubleshooting and problem-solving. Sometimes that means saying no. Anyone who ever had a chatbot agree with everything they said understands that AI often tells you what you want to hear.

6. Center work around human experience and emotion: Joy Evans Therapeutic Recreation Center in Washington, D.C.—the only public recreation center in the region offering therapeutic recreational programming—exemplifies the importance of designing for a range of human experiences. To make the center a welcoming and inclusive place for people of all ages and abilities, our designers needed a thorough human understanding of what made people feel safe, seen, and inspired. AI can grasp key tenets of accessibility and belonging abstractly, but doesn’t understand human vulnerability.

When we recognize and respect these messy parts of the process, we understand that human professionals can’t be replaced. It’s important we help our clients and customers understand this too, demonstrating how we can use the best of AI while emphasizing the value of human judgment and perspective.

#70013. Industry News: Why ‘you don’t have to use AI’ is the new AI pitch

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3012 w)
📖 Baca

Industry News: Why ‘you don’t have to use AI’ is the new AI pitch

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that watching Adobe’s keynote address at the 24th annual annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope it’s walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through.
  • According to recent reports, watching Adobe’s keynote address at the 24th annual annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope it’s walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through.
  • It has been revealed that at Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that watching Adobe’s keynote address at the 24th annual annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope it’s walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through. In both, there’s a desire to be AI-forward and skate to where the puck is going. At the same time, they need to deal with a hostile crowd—meaning the growing backlash against AI among many of their customers. At Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis. The company touted AI features, including ways to generate content directly in their Creative Cloud apps, such as Photoshop and Premiere. Adobe hyped up Firefly, which was then mostly associated with the company’s image models. In 2024, Adobe told the audience that “2024 will go down as the year that creativity changed forever.” In 2025, the headliners were a new Firefly image model and a lineup of third-party models from Google, OpenAI, Runway, and others, and “choice” mostly meant choosing which AI model to use. The lone nod to skeptics was a passing aside: “Of course, you can ignore it all as well.” This year, the tone shifted. In fact, one of the first things incoming CEO Anil Chakravarthy emphasized during the opening keynote was that owners didn’t have to use AI if they didn’t want to. “Some of you don’t want to have anything to do with AI,” he said, promising to give those users “the precision and control that you’re looking for, and the option to not use AI.” Instead of a new Firefly model number, the keynote spotlighted upgrades with no AI in them at all, like a rebuilt color mode in Premiere and Dynamic Text in Illustrator. Firefly is still an area of focus, but it’s evolved into a catch-all creative studio, more like Figma than an AI model. (Disclosure: Adobe paid for my travel to Max, though it had no input on this column.) AI-optional doesn’t mean AI-free None of this is to say Adobe is walking away from AI. Far from it: During that same keynote, Chakravarthy announced Adobe would be providing a way for AI services to access Creative Cloud applications directly through the model context protocol (MCP) standard. That means AI users will be able to have Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini act as an agent, effectively “driving” Photoshop and other Creative Cloud apps to edit projects, create content, and export files directly on their computers. The integrations go into private beta in early 2027. Adobe already provides an AI connector that works similarly, but the MCPs would take things to a new level of precision and control. Jesus Diaz has a great breakdown of exactly how they would work and what it means for creators. In addition, Adobe is building out its own agents: The new Creative Agent is essentially an Adobe chatbot where you can describe what you want and the agent handles the execution in the appropriate app. It’s now in beta inside Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io. All this makes it clear Adobe isn’t slowing down on AI. It has, however, recognized that a great bifurcation is taking place, one that’s affecting all industries to some extent, but especially the media. On the one hand, you have your AI skeptics, customers who are suspicious of AI generally and AI-generated or -assisted content specifically. And on the other, you have the AI enthusiasts, the ones who are using AI to enhance and speed up their work, including through tools from other companies. This is the AI tightrope, and all businesses will need to navigate it over the next few years. Not just because AI represents “the future” in some vague sense, but because, if it does, it opens up a new kind of customer. Now everyone knows kung-fu My business is actually a pretty good example of this. I use various software, including Photoshop and Premiere, to help produce content like The Media Copilot podcast. But I’m not a creator per se, and I’m probably using only about 10% of the features that would help my use case. For many, that skill gap is the difference between subscribing and not. But an agent that bridges the gap could mean Adobe customers are no longer just enthusiasts and experts. Suddenly we’re all Neo in the Matrix: just plug an agent into your workstream, and you know kung-fu. In fact, one of the keynote demos was more or less my exact workflow: an outside AI agent turning a long-form podcast into a batch of short clips for social. There’s also an urgency here, and again my use case is a good example. I’ve already begun offloading some of my production process to agents. Claude Code and OpenAI Codex are both excellent at analyzing workflows and recommending software solutions that they (not I) can operate. Often, it’s open-source software that gets the job done at virtually no cost other than the tokens I expend. And Adobe users can even employ computer use—where the AI uses your machine, just as you would—to operate the software. It’s messier than an MCP, but it gets the job done, and AI is getting better at this by the day. In other words, the AI world is moving toward agentic work, with or without Adobe. Businesses of all kinds are beginning to demand this kind of functionality, and even if open-source software is cheaper, there are advantages to using commercial software. Security, reliability, and auditability are all very notable to enterprises. And it’s mutually beneficial to Adobe, since the number of licenses those businesses buy will no longer be limited by the number of experts they have. Notably, the MCP integrations require the apps to be installed and licensed on the user’s machine. Even when an agent is the one driving Photoshop, someone is still paying for the seat. Media’s version of the same customer There’s a corollary here in media. As people turn more and more to AI answers for information, it means bots scrape all kinds of sites to find the best possible answer. A consequence of this is that niche sites—in particular B2B media—have become some of the most sought-after sources on the web. TollBit’s latest State of the Bots report ranks B2B and professional sites among the most heavily scraped categories it tracks, with scraping up 62% from Q2 2025 to Q4 2025. Their specialized knowledge might sometimes be impenetrable to mainstream audiences, but never to AI agents. They can swiftly parse the bits that are important and relevant, then break them down in a way that’s understandable to anyone. Just like with those Photoshop agents, lack of expertise is no longer a barrier to adoption. But what about those AI skeptics? They’re an important part of any company’s existing customer base, and they’ve made their views clear: They don’t want to see AI in the content they consume. I’ve written about the problem with AI tells in text, and the same goes for images and video: audiences consistently say they don’t like them. That doesn’t mean all AI is bad, and many Adobe AI-powered features garnered lots of applause at MAX. But it needs to be in the right context. A good rule of thumb: AI behind the scenes is generally OK, but generative content you need to be careful with. The audience research lines up almost exactly. In the Reuters Institute’s Generative AI and News Report 2025, only 12% of people said they were comfortable with news made entirely by AI, compared with 62% for news made entirely by humans. But 55% were fine with AI fixing spelling and grammar. Most media companies have arrived at a similar place. There are tantalizing opportunities for content to reach new audiences through AI search engines and agent protocols like MCP. At the same time, they need to tread lightly when implementing artificial intelligence in their own operations, lest they lose trust with their existing audience. That’s the AI tightrope, and staying balanced is obviously the trick to moving forward. Getting the agents to pay up But what’s on the other end? At least for Adobe, the answer is clearer: a new and potentially huge customer base who don’t want to use tools but are happy for their agents to. For media, the other end of the rope is murkier. The agents are already here, reading trade publications and national news alike, but most of them are still taking what they find without paying for it. AI apps send publishers a sliver of the traffic Google does, and the deals that would make up the difference are stuck in courtrooms and licensing negotiations. Adobe found a way to charge for the agents using its tools. Until the media figures out how to get agents to pay for the privilege of reading content, it’s walking the same tightrope, just without a net.

#70012. Breaking: Intel Diamond Rapids highlights signs of life in SC26 demo running live server

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (682 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Intel Diamond Rapids highlights signs of life in SC26 demo running live server

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly.
  • Industry observers note that the demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller.
  • Of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly. Most interesting was a running server at the CXL booth, showcasing a demo with a Diamond Rapids CPU. The server ran for the first day of the show, and upon returning to the booth, we were informed that it had been shut down due to noise complaints (it’s hard to mistake a running server). Elsewhere at Bull’s booth, a Diamond Rapids CPU was shown installed in a server behind a glass case. Notably, Intel didn’t have a Diamond Rapids demo, instead focusing most of its booth on Xeon 6+ and its new D270 GPU, otherwise known as Crescent Island.

Industry observers note that the demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller. If you’re unfamiliar, memory expansion via CXL is an increasingly common tactic to give multi-host environments access to a large pool of memory, breaking free of an individual server’s capacity via CXL. In the demo, Montage is showing off its memory expansion controller running across a Xeon 6 and a Diamond Rapids server, each sharing a pool of memory over CXL. CXL is an open standard, built atop PCIe.

Of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild. The 256 GB memory capacity shown doesn’t provide any hints, either. Intel has announced that Diamond Rapids will support 16-channel memory, with RDIMM support up to 8,000 MT/s and MRDIMM support up to 12,800 MT/s, matching AMD’s recent EPYC Venice CPUs. However, Intel hasn’t revealed capacity, though we anticipate the maximum capacity will be far above 256 GB – for context, last-gen Granite Rapids-AP supports up to 3 TB per socket.

Industry observers note that bull is a French server designer focused on HPC and AI infrastructure, and it revealed off two Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids chips installed in the Bullsquana XH31600 server. As expected for a 2P Diamond Rapids server, it supports 32 channels of DDR5 memory, and it’s designed for a liquid-cooled deployment.

Recent findings suggest that as you can see from the image, these aren’t production chips. They’re labeled with “Intel confidential,” and the code starts with “Q,” revealing that this is a sample. Originally, we expected to see Diamond Rapids in the second half of this year, perhaps around this time. However, in August, Intel revealed that Xeon 7 chips would launch in 2027.

Based on the various servers we saw and the live demo, it seems Intel is targeting a launch earlier in the year, likely in Q2; we expect a larger consumer focus in Q1. It could slip later into the year, though that seems very unlikely given that Diamond Rapids was already pushed back, and the insatiable demand for CPUs in AI data centers doesn’t appear to be drying up.

In a recent development, also pointing to a relatively quick release are the various servers we saw on the floor at SC26. Several partners showed off their next-gen servers built for Diamond Rapids CPU, sporting the LGA 9324 socket, including Dell and Asus (pictured above). However, Bull was the only vendor we could find that had an actual chip on display.

Diamond Rapids is Intel’s true next-gen CPU, following up on the E-core-only Xeon 6+ range that rolled out earlier this year. Diamond Rapids packs up to 256 P-cores, and it’s built on Intel’s performance-enhanced 18A-P node. The most interesting aspect of the chip is its topology, with Intel breaking from its previous layout and building something much similar to an EPYC CPU. The package features centralized memory and I/O, which were pushed out to the edges of the package with Granite Rapids. You can read more about the design of the chip in our Diamond Rapids recap from Hot Chips on Tom’s Hardware Premium.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

RTO means women risk doing the office housework all over again

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all.
  • Sources indicate that women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all.
  • Recent findings suggest that usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all. Now, old-fashioned assumptions about the unpaid work women are expected to take on in the office risk adding to that burden. Usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries. And it’s women who are more likely to do more domestic labor even when both partners are employed full time. One 2024 study of 3,000 US parents found that mothers took primary responsibility for 71% of household tasks requiring mental effort, compared with 45% for fathers. It happens at work, too, where it’s known as “office housework.” These are the unpaid, often unrecognized tasks that keep an organization running but rarely help the people doing them advance their careers. Women therefore can end up doing more work without getting any credit for it. And RTO might be making things worse. A study of 1,091 professional women in the US found that 31% reported experiencing everyday gender discrimination when working on-site, compared with 17% when working remotely. This included performing tasks that weren’t their responsibility. The results suggest that being physically present can expose women to more everyday gender discrimination and create more opportunities for these assumptions to surface. The problem is also evident in the UK. In a new survey of 2,000 working women and men by advocacy group Co-operatives UK, 22% of women said they’d been asked to do paperwork outside their role, 21% had been asked to clean or tidy the office, and 20% had been asked to make coffee for senior leaders. Overall, nearly half (49%) of women said they’d been asked more than once to do something outside their role, such as making tea or booking a meeting room. Women have been highlighting the problem on social media, sharing their experiences and how they push back against the assumption that they’ll take on these tasks. One content creator, Alex Schudy, said she had noticed colleagues using what she described as “weaponized incompetence” to try to get her to take notes in meetings, often by throwing her a compliment to disguise it. In her video on TikTok, she said she let the “silence linger” when one colleague suggested she do it because her handwriting was neat and she was “organized.” She politely declined, explaining that she needed to focus on presenting her part of the meeting. Someone else was designated the notetaker instead. Another creator, Anna Kennedy, described in a video how much office housework she had come to realise women were doing — from keeping track of action items and chasing colleagues to making sure feedback was acted upon. “Things that keep the machine moving fundamentally, but are not rewarded or seen in a performance review,” she said. “I’m never, I swear to God, never seeing men doing this kind of work.” As more employees settle back into office life, many hope there have been changes for the better, particularly around work-life balance and flexibility. But some of the oldest workplace habits seem stubbornly resistant to change, and it’s time women stopped being expected to pick up the slack. Ultimately, they shouldn’t have to spend their working days doing the jobs that keep everyone else organized, only to be left behind as everyone else speeds ahead.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motorola’s upcoming Razr Flex foldable is expected to have the same wide foldable form factor as Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, and upcoming leaks not only reveal its design, but hint at some key specs.

Ahead of its supposed 2027 debut, the Motorola Razr Flex has now leaked in a real-life image. The image shows the back of the phone with a dual-camera setup, Pixel-like camera bar, and a design that matches that short and stout look of Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo. It also pretty clearly lines up with past teasers of this device.

Rumor has it that the Razr Flex will be even smaller than Samsung or Apple’s wide foldables, and the proportions of this image make that all the more certain.

Beyond this, some regulatory leaks reveal key specs on the Motorola Razr Flex.

It has been revealed that the foldable will apparently run Android 17 out of the box – an revision that Razr Fold is only getting just now – and run on the Qualcomm SM8845 Pro chipset. Android Authority notes that this isn’t a chip that’s been unveiled yet, but it’s thought to be called “Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 Pro.”.

Recent findings suggest that other rumored specs include a 4.97-inch outer display, 6.92-inch inner display, 5,000 mAh battery, 12GB of RAM, and two 50MP cameras around back. Based on information from a past leak, the color variant pictured above is likely called “Coriander.”.

#70007. The future of live entertainment

The future of live entertainment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us.
  • Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us.
  • Amid this profound transformation, our desire for experiences that are deeply human has never been greater.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Change is in the air. Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us. Amid this profound transformation, our desire for experiences that are deeply human has never been greater. Technology can do so much, including simulating interaction and placing nearly limitless entertainment at our fingertips. But it cannot fully replicate formative live entertainment moments like the collective anticipation before a performance or the emotional release of thousands of people experiencing the same unforgettable moment together. Human beings are fundamentally social. We are drawn to one another and transformed by shared experience. Gathering is part of who we are. That fundamental human desire places us on the precipice of a cultural renaissance. Throughout history, moments of mass disruption have repeatedly created the conditions for extraordinary periods of advancement in art, science, architecture, technology, and design. These moments force societies to question familiar assumptions and search for new ways to understand one another. We are entering such a moment now. In this emerging age of artificiality, human creativity will command a new premium. So will presence. The experiences we cannot download, automate, or predict will become more valuable precisely because they are real. For designers (and any type of creative), this is an extraordinary opportunity. We have the ability—and responsibility—to shape the experiences that define the next era of culture. 4 IDEAS TO GUIDE THE NEXT ERA OF CULTURE History demonstrates that people are remarkably resilient. When confronted with uncertainty or moments of radical change, we search for reasons to believe in what comes next, then adapt accordingly. What follows are four ideas that can help ensure this latest cultural renaissance is a period of meaningful transformation that unites people globally for a shared purpose: connection. 1. The importance of optimism  That instinct remains powerful today. According to recent research from VML Intelligence, 69% of respondents regularly feel hopeful about the future. Beneath the anxiety surrounding technological and cultural change, optimism persists. That optimism matters because hope rarely remains an individual emotion. People seek opportunities to express it collectively. Live entertainment gives physical form to that desire. Watching Lionel Messi with his foot on the ball in the 90th minute of the FIFA World Cup, a stadium erupting in victory, a concert audience singing a chorus with Taylor Swift, or a theater falling completely silent at the same emotional moment reveals something profound. Emotion becomes amplified when it’s shared. The most successful venues build anticipation and entice participation. They create the conditions for strangers to feel connected. As optimism becomes a defining force in the next cultural era, the places that bring people together will become increasingly important expressions of collective possibility. 2. The return of real The renewed interest in analog experiences is already visible across culture. Vinyl records, tapes, and physical media have returned to prominence. Film cameras and Polaroids are reappearing at concerts and celebrations. Tactile pursuits such as journaling and knitting are attracting new generations. These behaviors are sometimes dismissed as nostalgia. But they represent something more consequential: a desire for agency and authenticity. It is a tangible connection in a world of infinite, algorithmically delivered content. People want experiences they can touch and remember. They want the imperfect and the unpredictable. They desire the unrepeatable. Live entertainment is the ultimate expression of that desire. No two performances are the same. No crowd produces the same energy. No professional athlete reacts in the same way in that critical winning moment. The possibility that something unexpected might happen is the source of its power. Designers are beginning to respond through spaces that encourage deeper presence and participation. Listening rooms, intimate performance spaces, flexible venues, and carefully choreographed social environments are creating new ways to experience music and culture together. In the age of artificiality, the real becomes rare. Rarity creates the ultimate value. 3. From experience to transformation This cultural recalibration aligns with B. Joseph Pine’s concept of the transformation economy. This is the idea that people increasingly seek experiences that change them. Businesses and institutions will increasingly be judged by what they provide and by whether the experiences they create feel meaningful and transformative. This is especially true in sports and live entertainment, where identity, ritual, and emotion are inseparable from the event itself. The 2026 FIFA World Cup offered a powerful expression of this idea. Supporters traveled from across the globe not simply to watch soccer, but to participate in one of humanity’s great, shared traditions. The matches mattered, but so did the pilgrimage, the gathering, the rituals, and the sense of belonging to a global community. The same principle exists at every scale, spanning the intimacy of a listening room to the collective roar of a stadium and everything in between. Each can become a place where human connection is forged, moments that become treasured memories. 4. A collective opportunity awaits The next era of live entertainment will be defined by how thoughtfully technology is used to deepen, not displace, the human experience. Our greatest opportunity is to design places that encourage people to look up from their devices, toward the performance and toward one another. Places that transform attendance into participation, audiences into communities, and fleeting moments into enduring memories. These places give physical form to the things artificial intelligence cannot manufacture; chief among them, authentic, spontaneous, and shared emotion. The conditions for a cultural renaissance are already here. Its character, however, is not predetermined. It will be shaped by the choices of many, including cultural and entertainment leaders. Let’s collectively embrace an opportunity to design and lead a new era. It’s one that doesn’t come often and can spark lasting impacts that will positively influence generations to come. Brian Mirakian is senior principal at Populous.

  • Silicon Motion introduced its high-end MonTitan SM8466 enterprise SSD controller designed for next-generation data center and hyperscale storage applications at FMS 2025.
  • In a recent development, to improve performance and reduce latency, Silicon Motion has developed its Separate Command Architecture (SCA), which separates command and address transmission paths within the NAND interface to improve parallelism and increase effective throughput.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silicon Motion is showing off its PCIe 6.0 SSD controller for data center applications for the first time at the SC26 conference in Chicago. The final iteration of Silicon Motion's SM8466 controller was taped out recently, and drives based on the chip are due in late 2027 or early 2028. However, the latest controller also has a secret weapon designed to ensure consistent performance of SSDs under concurrent workloads that may set it apart from competitors.

Silicon Motion introduced its high-end MonTitan SM8466 enterprise SSD controller designed for next-generation data center and hyperscale storage applications at FMS 2025. The controller features a PCIe 6.x x4 host interface and 16 NAND channels to enable sequential transfer speeds of up to 28 GB/s, random performance of up to 7 million 4K IOPS, and capacities of up to 512 TB and beyond as newer 3D NAND devices emerge. Just like other high-end data center-grade SSD controllers released in recent years, the SM8466 complies with NVMe 2.0 and OCP NVMe 2.5 SSD specifications.

In a recent development, to improve performance and reduce latency, Silicon Motion has developed its Separate Command Architecture (SCA), which separates command and address transmission paths within the NAND interface to improve parallelism and increase effective throughput. Additionally, the controller supports Silicon Motion's 2nd Generation PerformaShape technology, which enables programmable performance limits and predictable quality of service (QoS) across concurrent workloads, which is arguably its most important differentiator against rivals who rely on different methods of guaranteeing performance.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to its performance chops, the MonTitan SM8466 incorporates advanced error correction, virtualization, data protection, and security features. The controller's error correction engine supports low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with 4KiB codewords and Silicon Motion's 16KiB Collaborative Codeword (CoCo) technology to improve data integrity and reliability with advanced NAND flash memory. The controller also supports Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV), MPF virtualization, SMART diagnostics, and comprehensive data protection mechanisms. Security capabilities include Secure Boot, AES-256 encryption, TCG Opal compatibility, and firmware attestation. Together, these features make the SM8466 suitable for high-capacity data center drives that are expected to deliver high performance, predictable latency, and reliable operation under demanding data center workloads.

It has been revealed that silicon Motion's 2nd Generation PerformaShape technology builds upon the original PerformaShape architecture introduced with the firm's PCIe 5.0-based MonTitan SM8366 enterprise SSD controller several years ago. The 1st Generation implementation uses dedicated hardware accelerators and two-stage leaky-bucket regulators to control read and write performance in terms of IOPS and throughput, both for individual workloads and for the SSD as a whole. This approach enables data center operators to prevent one workload from monopolizing SSD resources at the expense of others.

Sources indicate that performaShape 2 retains these capabilities but doubles the number of supported quality-of-service (QoS) sets from 256 to 512 and introduces more sophisticated performance controls to accommodate a larger number of concurrent workloads with different requirements. One of the key additions to PerformaShape 2 is Multi-Dimensional Shaping, which enables the controller to coordinate performance limits across multiple I/O characteristics rather than enforce each limit independently. This gives data center operators greater flexibility when allocating SSD resources among applications with different performance requirements.

According to recent reports, another crucial enhancement of PerformaShape 2 is support for NVMe TP4176, a proposed extension to the NVMe specification that aims to standardize performance management and QoS controls. Whereas the original PerformaShape relies on Silicon Motion's vendor-specific NVMe commands and a dedicated host driver, TP4176 could eventually enable compatible host software to configure performance policies through a standardized mechanism. The technology is particularly relevant for cloud environments where SSDs serve numerous virtual machines, containers, and applications whose storage requirements can change considerably over time, according to the organization.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the days of MySpace’s Top 8, social media has made it easy to hurt your friends’ feelings. Some platforms make it easy to judge relative friendship, like Snapchat’s publicly viewable “Best Friends” feature. Instagram, however, keeps owners’ social dynamics under wraps from one another, with accounts unable to see when someone unfollows them. Instagram head Adam Mosseri has previously stated the platform hasn’t introduced a “who unfollowed me” feature so that users feel free to unfollow whomever they please without fear of judgment or tension. But a upcoming tool from Instagram’s parent organization Meta is shaking things up. Its AI assistant Muse has an apparently petty personality under its cute and cuddly exterior—and it’s happy to help users spot who isn’t following them back and then unfollow them en masse. How Muse can purge your Instagram Social media users have discovered that Muse can sort through the people they follow on Instagram and point out any non-mutual connections. Though third-party apps have offered similar features in the past, they’re notorious for getting accounts flagged and taken down from Instagram. Muse, as an in-house app, doesn’t pose the same risk. One Instagram user who tried out the feature, Khalil Roberts, told Wired about his experience using Muse. Roberts gave Muse the prompt, “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on Instagram, and can you unfollow them for me.” It swiftly returned an Excel spreadsheet with 151 accounts that fit his criteria, then asked if he wanted to follow through on unfollowing them. Roberts was among the chorus on social media singing Muse’s praises for letting them purge such accounts so easily. “I just cleared 80+ chopped hos who thought I was a fan,” one user posted. “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG,” another user boasted, crediting Muse in a follow-up post. Meta’s secret menu Though Muse’s potential for pettiness is a much-requested feature, it’s only being spread through word of mouth. Meta itself isn’t advertising the capability—or at least not anymore. In October, Los Angeles-based social media consultant Rachel Karten noticed a Meta ad on Instagram touting that Muse could let users “see who unfollowed you each week.” “I get that this is technically a requested feature but wouldn’t it lead to more resentment towards your own platform?” Karten asked in a post sharing a screenshot of the ad. i get that this is technically a requested feature but wouldn’t it lead to more resentment towards your own platform? pic.twitter.com/SbM6VdcdhV— Rachel Karten (@milkkarten) October 24, 2026 Indeed, Instagram has since taken down the ad, as a Meta representative confirmed to Business Insider. Still, the feature remains active in Muse—as long as users know to ask for it.

In a recent development, picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

In a recent development, shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

It has been revealed that whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

Recent findings suggest that wooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

Industry observers note that bigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Industry observers note that medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company notes you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Sources indicate that own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pakistan's telecommunications authority, the PTA, has confirmed that internet connectivity concerns affecting the country's residents are related to the failure of an international submarine cable. SEA-ME-WE 5 is located almost seven miles off the coast of Pakistan, near the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz, and connects the region with European networks via the Middle East. The TWA notes that the outage may have caused intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality, with Transworld Associates (TWA) working to identify the cause of the issue. No timeframe has been provided for when a fix will be available yet, but for now, internet traffic has been rerouted to minimize the impact of the outage.

Sources indicate that the outage comes weeks after the Islamic Republic of Iran described several undersea fiber cables that run through the Strait of Hormuz as "legitimate newly introduced targets" in the ongoing tensions in the area. February's start of military action by the United States, Israel, and others has made the Strait of Hormuz a household name in recent months. General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, pointed out that as many as seven "large cables pass beneath the Strait of Hormuz, and all internet and commercial data pass through them," going on to say they are "legitimate" targets for the group.

Recent findings suggest that one of the international submarine cable systems, the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5), have reported a fault at about 11 KM from Pakistan shore which may cause some internet owners to experience intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality. Transworld Associates (TWA) is coordinating with the SMW5 Consortium to identify the root cause of the fault and determine the Estimated Time for Restoration (ETTR). In the meantime, internet traffic is being rerouted through alternative international links to minimise the impact and ensure service continuity to the greatest extent possible. #SMW5 #SubmarineCableFault #InternetDisruption #InternetUpdate #PakistanInternet #ConnectivityUpdate #InternetServices #DigitalPakistan #PTA #TransworldAssociates #TelecomUpdate #NetworkRestoration #StayConnected #InternetConnectivityNovember 18, 2026.

Notably, the SEA-ME-WE 5 cable does run through the Strait of Hormuz, although it should be stressed that there is currently no indication that this outage was caused by any act of sabotage. However, that is no doubt something that the TWA investigation will seek to confirm before it can apply whatever fix is necessary to fully restore services for those in the region.

Undersea cables are vital for maintaining connectivity between nations and continents, and Iran isn't the only one to have taken note. A Russian ship was chased from British waters by a Royal Navy attack helicopter earlier this year after it was found less than a mile from five undersea cables. The ship was in the area for 14 hours, and the cables it was near happened to connect the UK with Spain, Portugal, Canada, and the United States.

Industry News: America’s next quantum breakthrough: The factory floor

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that building a quantum computing firm has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist.
  • Recent findings suggest that building a quantum computing organization has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist.
  • Industry observers note that for years, the prevailing wisdom in technology was to focus on what you do best and outsource the rest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that building a quantum computing firm has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist. Developing a new technology is one challenge. Figuring out how to manufacture it reliably, at scale, is another. And the second can be every bit as difficult as the first. For years, the prevailing wisdom in technology was to focus on what you do best and outsource the rest. It made good business sense. Building manufacturing capacity is expensive, complicated, and often far removed from the work that inspired someone to start a technology company in the first place. But that approach comes with a tradeoff. When you depend on someone else to manufacture your technology, you also depend on their capabilities, priorities, and timelines. For an emerging industry like quantum information, those dependencies can become significant obstacles. And I believe they have implications well beyond any one company. A LESSON WE’VE ALREADY LEARNED The United States has seen what happens when technological innovation and manufacturing become separated. American companies designed many of the advanced semiconductors powering today’s AI revolution, but much of the manufacturing capacity needed to produce them was developed overseas. That arrangement supported decades of innovation and economic growth. It also created dependencies that have become increasingly difficult to ignore. Now, the U.S. is investing heavily in rebuilding domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity. It’s a difficult and expensive undertaking, and one that will take years to fully realize. Quantum technologies give us an opportunity to think about these challenges earlier in an industry’s development. The U.S. has extraordinary strengths in quantum science. Our universities, national laboratories, and private companies have helped advance the field for decades. But the path from a scientific breakthrough to a useful product requires more than research. Much more. It requires specialized materials, fabrication processes, engineering expertise, and the ability to produce increasingly complex technologies consistently and economically. Those capabilities need to develop alongside science. WHY WE CHOSE TO BUILD I’ve experienced this challenge firsthand at Quantum Computing Inc. Our work in quantum photonics depends on highly specialized manufacturing processes. As we developed our technology, we had to think carefully about how much of our future we wanted to depend on outside manufacturing partners. For a growing company, investing in your own manufacturing capabilities is a consequential decision. It requires capital, specialized expertise, and a willingness to take on responsibilities that extend well beyond research and product development. We ultimately decided to build and acquire manufacturing capacity because we believe greater control over the critical and proprietary processes is essential to our long-term strategy. For other processes, we will leverage existing manufacturing capabilities and collaborate with industry partners to build a robust, reliable, and sustainable supply chain. We also see an opportunity to contribute to the broader ecosystem by making our manufacturing capabilities available to others. The quantum opportunity is far bigger than any one company. Advancing the industry will require collaboration and shared capabilities that benefit all of us. It’s time to work together to build that foundation and accelerate the growth of the quantum industry. NO ONE MANUFACTURING MODEL That decision has shaped how I think about innovation. When researchers and engineers have closer access to manufacturing, they can learn from what happens during fabrication and use that knowledge to improve the next design. Manufacturing becomes part of the development process itself. The experience gained along the way can be just as valuable as the equipment. There is no single manufacturing model that makes sense for every quantum company. Different technologies have different requirements, and outside foundries and specialized partners remain important. But access to reliable manufacturing capacity can have a profound influence on how rapidly an idea becomes something useful. BUILD AN INDUSTRY, NOT JUST A TECHNOLOGY Washington D.C. is beginning to recognize this challenge. A June executive order addressing quantum technology calls for strengthening domestic manufacturing capabilities and expanding partnerships between government and private industry. I welcome that attention. But building a manufacturing base requires more than funding announcements and policy commitments. It takes facilities, equipment, specialized talent, and years of experience developing processes that work consistently. It also requires demand from companies that are ready to move technologies out of the laboratory and into practical use. Other countries recognize the importance of these capabilities, with many having committed substantial resources to quantum technology. The United States has important advantages in research, entrepreneurship, and private investment. We should be building on those strengths now. That doesn’t mean every component needs to be manufactured domestically. International partnerships and global supply chains will continue to play important roles. But we should be deliberate about which capabilities are essential to our technological independence, making sure we have the capacity to develop and sustain them. FINAL THOUGHTS I’ve spent much of my career working to advance quantum technology. Like many scientists, I was initially drawn to the possibilities of what we could discover and what those discoveries make possible. Today, I spend just as much time thinking about what it takes to turn those possibilities into something people can use. That means manufacturing, supply chains, engineering, and all the difficult work that follows a breakthrough. The U.S. has an extraordinary foundation in quantum science. What we do with that advantage now matters. We need to invest in the ability to manufacture these technologies with the same conviction and intensity we brought to discovering them. Yuping Huang is CEO of Quantum Computing Inc.

Recent findings suggest that building a quantum computing organization has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist. Developing a new technology is one challenge. Figuring out how to manufacture it reliably, at scale, is another. And the second can be every bit as difficult as the first.

Industry observers note that for years, the prevailing wisdom in technology was to focus on what you do best and outsource the rest. It made good business sense. Building manufacturing capacity is expensive, complicated, and often far removed from the work that inspired someone to start a technology tech giant in the first place.

Sources indicate that but that approach comes with a tradeoff. When you depend on someone else to manufacture your technology, you also depend on their capabilities, priorities, and timelines.

For an emerging industry like quantum information, those dependencies can become significant obstacles. And I believe they have implications well beyond any one organization.

The United States has seen what happens when technological innovation and manufacturing become separated.

American companies designed many of the advanced semiconductors powering today’s AI revolution, but much of the manufacturing capacity needed to produce them was developed overseas. That arrangement supported decades of innovation and economic growth. It also created dependencies that have become increasingly difficult to ignore.

Now, the U.S. is investing heavily in rebuilding domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity. It’s a difficult and expensive undertaking, and one that will take years to fully realize.

Quantum technologies give us an opportunity to think about these challenges earlier in an industry’s development.

The U.S. has extraordinary strengths in quantum science. Our universities, national laboratories, and private companies have helped advance the field for decades. But the path from a scientific breakthrough to a useful product requires more than research. Much more. It requires specialized materials, fabrication processes, engineering expertise, and the ability to produce increasingly complex technologies consistently and economically.

Those capabilities need to develop alongside science.

I’ve experienced this challenge firsthand at Quantum Computing Inc. Our work in quantum photonics depends on highly specialized manufacturing processes. As we developed our technology, we had to think carefully about how much of our future we wanted to depend on outside manufacturing partners.

For a growing company, investing in your own manufacturing capabilities is a consequential decision. It requires capital, specialized expertise, and a willingness to take on responsibilities that extend well beyond research and product development.

Recent findings suggest that we ultimately decided to build and acquire manufacturing capacity because we believe greater control over the critical and proprietary processes is essential to our long-term strategy. For other processes, we will leverage existing manufacturing capabilities and collaborate with industry partners to build a robust, reliable, and sustainable supply chain.

We also see an opportunity to contribute to the broader ecosystem by making our manufacturing capabilities available to others. The quantum opportunity is far bigger than any one company. Advancing the industry will require collaboration and shared capabilities that benefit all of us. It’s time to work together to build that foundation and accelerate the growth of the quantum industry.

That decision has shaped how I think about innovation.

When researchers and engineers have closer access to manufacturing, they can learn from what happens during fabrication and use that knowledge to improve the next design. Manufacturing becomes part of the development process itself. The experience gained along the way can be just as valuable as the equipment.

There is no single manufacturing model that makes sense for every quantum firm. Different technologies have different requirements, and outside foundries and specialized partners remain vital. But access to reliable manufacturing capacity can have a profound influence on how quickly an idea becomes something useful.

Washington D.C. is beginning to recognize this challenge. A June executive order addressing quantum technology calls for strengthening domestic manufacturing capabilities and expanding partnerships between government and private industry.

I welcome that attention. But building a manufacturing base requires more than funding announcements and policy commitments. It takes facilities, equipment, specialized talent, and years of experience developing processes that work consistently. It also requires demand from companies that are ready to move technologies out of the laboratory and into practical use.

Other countries recognize the importance of these capabilities, with many having committed substantial resources to quantum technology. The United States has important advantages in research, entrepreneurship, and private investment. We should be building on those strengths now.

That doesn’t mean every component needs to be manufactured domestically. International partnerships and global supply chains will continue to play important roles. But we should be deliberate about which capabilities are essential to our technological independence, making sure we have the capacity to develop and sustain them.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve spent much of my career working to advance quantum technology. Like many scientists, I was initially drawn to the possibilities of what we could discover and what those discoveries make possible.

Today, I spend just as much time thinking about what it takes to turn those possibilities into something people can use. That means manufacturing, supply chains, engineering, and all the difficult work that follows a breakthrough.

Sources indicate that the U.S. has an extraordinary foundation in quantum science. What we do with that advantage now matters. We need to invest in the ability to manufacture these technologies with the same conviction and intensity we brought to discovering them.

Yuping Huang is CEO of Quantum Computing Inc.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, remarked on Thursday that yields of chips made using the tech giant's latest 18A (1.8nm-class) fabrication process have achieved 70%, which is more or less in line with what one would expect from an all-newly introduced manufacturing technology at this stage of its ramp. In addition, Intel and Microsoft have signed an agreement under which Microsoft will secure Intel Xeon supply capacity for years to come and will use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology for in-house silicon.

"When I took over [as CEO in March, 2025], 18A yield was horrible; now we are at 70%," Lip-Bu Tan stated at the TomorrowX conference (via @firesidealpha).

According to recent reports, lip-Bu Tan did not specify whether he meant functional yield, parametric yield, or percentage of sellable silicon. However, it is reasonable to expect a CEO of a semiconductor tech giant to talk about functional die yield, the percentage of dies that pass basic electrical and functional testing.

Intel began volume production of compute tiles of its Core Ultra 300-series CPUs codenamed Panther Lake using 18A in the second half of 2025, so a 70% functional yield seems decent at this stage of the product ramp, though for Intel's economics a lot depends on parametric yield and how many advanced SKUs of Core Ultra 300-series 'Panther Lake' processors Intel can supply to customers at a premium. The same applies to Intel's Xeon 6+ Clearwater Forest processors with up to 288 cores that are in high-volume production now and which use 18A-based compute chiplets along with Foveros Direct 3D stacking.

In addition to announcing an important 18A milestone, Intel also signed a long-term agreement with Microsoft, under which the latter will secure multi-year Intel Xeon supply capacity, including supply of next-generation Xeon processors codenamed Diamond Rapids, and will use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology for multi-chiplet data center solutions developed in-house.

The EMIB agreement is arguably the biggest news. Microsoft is the first company to publicly commit to Intel's advanced packaging technology for its own silicon (i.e., it does not mean that Microsoft is the first third party to use EMIB; it is the first party to confirm usage of EMIB), which represents a significant commercial development for Intel Foundry in terms of publicity. However, the announcement does not identify the processors involved, their manufacturing process, production volumes, or deployment schedule. Microsoft was the first company to commit to use Intel's 18A for its data center silicon in 2024, though it is unclear whether the newly announced EMIB packaging agreement relates to the same solution or not. As the majority of high-end data center solutions tend to use multi-chiplet design, it is reasonable to expect Microsoft's future solutions for data centers to use EMIB for multi-die processors.

"Through use of our advanced packaging capabilities with EMIB to scale future generations of Azure infrastructure, Intel and Microsoft can combine the flexibility of heterogeneous integration with the manufacturing scale required for the AI era — giving customers newly introduced levels of performance and economics when interacting with Azure," said Naga Chandrasekaran, EVP, Chief Technology and Operations Officer and General Manager of Intel Foundry.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Sources indicate that the Xeon agreement provides Intel with greater visibility into future server CPU demand. Importantly, Microsoft has committed to using Intel's next-generation Xeon 'Diamond Rapids,' although the announcement does not disclose purchase volumes or financial terms.

Industry observers note that the collaboration extends beyond processor procurement and EMIB. Specifically, Intel and Microsoft are jointly developing infrastructure capabilities that encompass processor architecture, heterogeneous integration, CXL memory expansion, QuickAssist Technology (QAT) acceleration, and Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) security.

AI adoption could disproportionately harm Black and Latino workers

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest.
  • It has been revealed that it has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest.
  • Sources indicate that the effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest. While entry level roles are, in fact, on the decline in tech and finance—and employers continue to use AI as a rationale for layoffs—there is ample evidence that rapid AI adoption could interrupt pathways for workers without college degrees. The effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted. Some of the jobs that have been deemed “highly exposed” to AI, including clerical and administrative roles, are largely dominated by women, and a newly introduced report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility posits that Black and Latino workers could also face major consequences. The report finds that Black and Latino workers are overrepresented in the sectors where automation and AI adoption will supplant work altogether, rather than augment work. While the overall rate of AI adoption is relatively stable across different demographics, Black and Latino workers will be affected more acutely by job displacement. Across working hours that are impacted by AI adoption, 40% of hours performed by Black workers and 41% by Latino workers will be displaced (as compared to 37% among white workers.)  That may not seem like a huge gap. But as the report points out, many of the jobs that are most exposed to AI have historically been pathways to the middle class, making them crucial drivers of social mobility across communities that have faced systemic barriers to entry. Black workers, in particular, dominate six jobs that are likely to see the biggest decline in labor demand, according to McKinsey, including postal mail carriers and customer service representatives; Latino workers are also especially likely to hold some of those jobs, namely dishwashers and hand packers. Black and Latino workers—along with those in rural regions—are also much more likely to be in jobs that involve physical labor, which are more vulnerable to being automated through robotics and other AI-enabled systems. On the whole, lower wage workers will face the greatest impact and are 7.6 times as likely to need to transition into a new job when compared to higher wage workers; people without a college degree are also 1.8 times more likely to need to do the same. Meanwhile, white workers are better positioned to both avoid this level of AI disruption and actually benefit from AI adoption in a number of ways. It’s not just that they’re more likely to hold jobs where AI will likely enhance their work, boosting productivity rather than replacing employees outright. When compared to their Black and Latino counterparts, white workers are also 30-50% more likely to work in the industries where private capital will be deployed, yielding more jobs and wealth creation, the McKinsey report states. That means white workers already have more of a foothold in jobs involving robotics or semiconductors or biotech, setting them up for success as hundreds of billions of dollars pour into those industries.(Look no further than the Anthropic IPO this week, which has created thousands of millionaires.)  In other words: Without broader policy changes or reskilling initiatives, many Black and Latino workers may be both forced out of their jobs and locked out of opportunities to cash in on the AI boom.

What is Model Routing in AI?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
